Feedback/Query: The home page currently shows eight-plus sections competing for attention at once — a live-class banner, jump-back-in card, four course cards, the momentum widget, rings, an AI promo, and two separate lists further down. It should collapse to a single dynamic card that answers "what do I do right now," ordered live class, then something due soon, then a lecture to resume, then a calm state. The harder design question is the tie-break: what shows when a class is live AND an assignment is due within the hour — the logic needs an explicit precedence rule, not just a list of conditions that happens to work in the demo data. Also worth designing deliberately: the calm "nothing urgent" state for a brand-new student with zero courses yet loaded, which is a real state during add/drop week, not just an edge case to shrug off.

The AI Tutor promo card should go — a student who already has full access shouldn't be marketed a feature they own. Worth doing a pass beyond just that one card for any other place "AI edition" or upgrade-style badging shows up where the student has nothing to actually upgrade to; that kind of leftover marketing language undercuts the "this is your real department" feeling the whole product is going for.

Grades should open with plain standing — "you're doing fine" or "CSE110 needs attention" — with the breakdown a tap away, not a dense table as the first thing seen. Two states need explicit design, not just the happy path: the start of term when no grades exist yet, which shouldn't read as a scary blank dashboard, and a final grade that's deliberately withheld until it's certified — the wording there matters a lot, because to an anxious student a withheld grade can easily read as a missing or broken one if it's not framed clearly.

A "what do I need on the final" tool is probably the single most-requested feature on any grades page a student actually uses, and it doesn't exist today. It needs to handle a few real cases correctly: courses with different weighting schemes, pass/fail courses where a numeric projection doesn't make sense, and — most important — a student who's already barred from finals on attendance grounds, where showing a hypothetical grade at all would be actively misleading.

Tapping a ring should go straight to the action that closes it rather than a detail page — Absorb to the lecture, Retrieve to practice, Apply to the next assignment. The thing to design for is what happens when there's genuinely nothing left to do for that ring today: no unwatched lecture, no more practice available. It can't dead-end, and with four enrolled courses there also needs a sensible default for which course's content it opens when more than one qualifies, rather than defaulting to alphabetical.

Right now the Absorb ring rewards time spent with a video open, which can be gamed by playing something at 2x with no attention at all, or just leaving a tab open. A light attention or recall check would make the metric mean something, but it has to be built carefully — it shouldn't penalize a student legitimately reviewing at 2x, someone who watches slower for genuine reasons, or a student on the low-bandwidth setting who may not even be streaming full video.

Tutor should remember the last course and topic and open straight into it instead of showing a picker every time. Worth deciding now, before a real backend exists, whether that memory lives per-device (today's likely local-storage answer) or per-account — a student switching from phone to laptop between classes is a completely normal case, and losing context on device switch would undercut the whole point of the fix.

There's currently no way for a student to flag a Tutor answer as wrong, and for a CS audience that will actively try to break it, that gap will get found fast. A visible correction loop — flag, review, fix — builds more credibility than pretending errors don't happen. The open design question is what happens to the same wrong answer for the next student who asks the same thing before a human's reviewed it; routing flagged answers into the same review queue Copilot already uses for teacher-approved content is probably the cleanest answer.

Down to Home, Courses, Grades, Tutor, and Profile, with Schedule and Practice folded into Courses and Settings/Usage into Profile. Worth keeping in mind for whenever group work ships: a student who's also leading a team project may need a nav destination that doesn't exist yet, so it's worth not over-optimizing the sidebar down to a count that has no room to grow.

There's no add/drop flow anywhere in the product, and this is the single highest-frequency, highest-anxiety thing a student does each term — seat scrambles, prerequisite conflicts, advising holds. If it's built rather than deep-linked to BRACU's existing system, it needs to model prerequisite chains, waitlists for full sections, and the genuinely cross-enrolled students the PRD itself flags (four of them this term) — those are exactly the cases a naive add/drop form breaks on first.

Nowhere in the current data model is there a notion of a team — no formation, no shared submission, no peer input — despite CSE courses running heavily on labs and group projects. If this gets built, two things need answers from day one: how uneven participation within a team gets surfaced (some form of individual contribution signal, not just a shared grade), and what happens to a team's submission when a member drops the course mid-term.

This is culturally one of the most-wanted features for BRAC exam prep and it doesn't exist yet. The real complexity isn't the UI, it's the policy underneath it: past papers are often faculty-owned material, so there needs to be a clear answer on who can upload and curate them, and whether worked solutions are included — an unmoderated answer bank is an academic-integrity risk, not just a content feature.

As a generic forum, this loses to the WhatsApp and Facebook groups students already run, because those are faster and more social. Before investing further, it's worth deciding what this actually is: an official, TA-answered, searchable Q&A archive that persists past the semester — genuinely useful during exam week in a way an ephemeral chat isn't — or an attempt at a social space, which is a different product with different moderation needs. Building it as an unclear hybrid of both is the outcome to avoid.

The live-class interface — chat, raise-hand, adaptive quality — is fully built out visually, but no actual video is streaming behind it yet; that needs a real backend (Agora, LiveKit, or similar) before any real class can run on it. Once it is real, the case worth planning for is a mid-class connection drop: does the student get a clear reconnect path, does the recording keep going even if their personal stream cuts out, and does behavior differ for someone already on the low-bandwidth setting.

Today there's an in-app bell and an email digest, but nothing reaches a student's phone directly, and a browser tab notification will consistently lose the race against a WhatsApp buzz. A WhatsApp Business API or local SMS channel would close that gap, but it needs frequency limits from the start so it doesn't become another ignored institutional broadcast list, plus a fallback to email for any student who hasn't registered a phone number yet during onboarding.

A one-at-a-time review flow — full-screen submission, the AI's draft score and feedback visible, approve and auto-advance, a visible progress bar, a genuine completion state at the end — would meaningfully cut the cognitive load of a nine-item queue. Two cases worth designing for explicitly: a teacher who disagrees sharply with the AI's draft score (code tests pass but the approach is wrong by the rubric) needs an override that doesn't feel like fighting the tool, and a late or resubmitted piece of work landing mid-session shouldn't disrupt the flow the teacher's already in.

Moving "generate a quiz for this chapter" onto the course content page itself, instead of a separate trip to Copilot with manual material selection, removes real friction. The thing to handle explicitly is a chapter with no uploaded material yet — the button should degrade to "upload your slides first" rather than generating from nothing or producing something that looks grounded but isn't.

Every at-risk flag needs something attached to it — a pre-drafted check-in message, a link to the student's profile, an option to flag the advisor — because a flag with no action attached mostly just creates anxiety for the teacher looking at it. Worth capping how often the same student gets flagged for outreach in a short window too; a well-meaning check-in message sent every week to the same struggling student stops being support and starts being noise.

Down to Home, Courses, Grading, Copilot, and Profile, with Record and Live becoming action buttons rather than sidebar destinations. Worth checking what a faculty member with zero sections this term — someone on sabbatical or in an admin-only role — actually sees; the grading queue and home cockpit shouldn't render as if something's broken just because there's genuinely nothing to grade.

Dr. Kamrul Hasan needs to be findable searching "Kamrul" or "Hasan" in the faculty picker — this is the emotional center of the pitch, the moment an evaluator finds themselves in their own department's data. Worth thinking through what the other 266 faculty see when they search their own name in the same picker, since in a room full of real BRAC faculty, everyone will try that first, and an empty or generic result for everyone but Kamrul undercuts the moment for the rest of the room.

Once Kamrul is findable, the corollary rule needs verifying: choosing any other name in the picker should only change what's displayed — the name, title, email — never re-filter the underlying teaching data. This is the mechanic that lets any evaluator "be" a professor and still see a complete class, and it's exactly the kind of rule that's invisible while it holds and only shows up as a problem once it silently breaks.

The recording studio's controls are real, but there's no topic-tagging option anywhere on the page, even though the product describes tagging a recording to a curriculum topic so it surfaces in the right place for students. Worth deciding the retag case too — if a teacher tags an already-published recording to a new topic later, does it retroactively appear for students who already watched and marked it done, or only for new viewers going forward.

The export button exists and is labeled correctly; what hasn't been confirmed is what the file actually contains for a section with a withheld or not-yet-released final grade. The case that matters here isn't a blank cell — it's whether the export could accidentally include a draft AI-suggested score that a teacher hasn't approved yet, which would be a real integrity problem given how much the product's credibility rests on this being the one genuinely functional export.

The rule that a teacher's private Momentum is never visible to the administrator needs to hold everywhere, including indirectly — worth specifically checking whether the Analyst could ever surface something correlated with it, for instance if a chair asks a question like "which teacher is least active," since that's a case where the underlying data could leak the intent of the rule even while technically not showing the Momentum score itself.

Splitting the home into a prominent "needs your decision" zone and a collapsed department-health summary below is the right instinct. Worth deciding a secondary sort for the case where two urgent items land on the same day with equal weight — an eligibility lock deadline and a certification deadline both due today, say — so the chair isn't left guessing which one actually needs attention first.

When nothing needs a decision, the Analyst's query box should become the actual hero of the home page rather than staying tucked in the sidebar. Worth checking the transition case specifically: if a new at-risk flag appears while that calm "ask anything" state is showing, does the page correctly snap back into decision mode on its own, or does the chair have to refresh before noticing something changed underneath them.

Only six of the ten named question types even show up as suggested chips today — department summary, worst attendance, lowest marks, at-risk, weakest course, teacher load. Eligibility-barred, certification-pending, top-marks, and term-compare need to be tried by typing them directly, and ideally get surfaced as chips too. Also worth defining behavior for a genuinely ambiguous or multi-part question — "who's at risk in CSE110 and how has the pass rate trended" — since it's not obvious today whether it answers one part and silently drops the rest, or handles it gracefully, and a sharp faculty member in the room will absolutely try exactly this kind of question.

Sections should sort with anomalies first rather than by section number, with clean sections labeled routine and a batch action to certify all of them at once. The sort needs to weigh more than one flag type though — a section with a clean pass rate but a real attendance anomaly shouldn't get buried under "routine" just because the headline number looks fine.

The product states repeatedly that every decision is logged, but there's no screen anywhere that actually shows that log to anyone — a registrar evaluating this for governance will ask where it lives. Worth deciding who gets to see it (chair only, or does a coordinator or an external auditor need read access too) and whether a return decision captures the reason, since "returned, no reason given" isn't useful to anyone looking back at it months later.

The "This term" tab — staffing, capacity, publishing — is real and working; Curriculum and Policy haven't been individually checked yet and should be before this is shown live. The specific case worth testing on Policy: if the 70% attendance threshold gets edited mid-term, does that retroactively re-run eligibility for students already evaluated under the old number, or only apply going forward — that's exactly the kind of policy-edit question that needs a tested, explicit answer rather than an assumed one.

The home should lead with a records-completeness checklist rather than with handoffs to the chair, since "is the data clean" is the actual question a coordinator opens the page asking. Worth designing the very first day of a term separately — a brand-new department being onboarded will show a checklist full of zeros, and that needs to read as "just getting started" rather than "something's broken."

Showing a preview after a file drop — how many will be added, how many already exist, how many have errors — before anything commits is the right call. The case worth handling explicitly is a near-duplicate row: same student ID but a different section. Treating that as a silent skip could quietly drop a legitimate section change instead of surfacing it as something that needs a decision.

The bulk-select and bulk-action bar, plus the add/edit form's uniqueness validation, haven't been exercised yet. Worth testing what happens when a bulk selection accidentally spans both faculty and student rows, or includes a record someone else has open for editing at the same moment — a bulk delete or bulk edit needs to be safe against that kind of overlap, not just fast.

Right now neither the keyboard shortcut nor a click on the search bar opens anything — it's the most visible example in the product of a control that looks interactive and does nothing, and it should be the very first thing fixed. Once it works, worth deciding what happens when a search matches nothing in the current role's world but would match something in a role the same person could switch to — a student searching a faculty member's name, for instance — since a graceful "did you mean to switch views" is a much better outcome than a flat no-results state.

A working theme control — auto, light, dark — already exists on the settings page; it's just not in the header where anyone looking for it would check first. The fix is moving it, not building it. Worth making sure the header control and the settings control read and write the same single source of truth, so a student can't end up with the two disagreeing about which theme is actually active.

Section: A Pattern Bug, Not Three Bugs
Feedback/Query: Three z-index and modal-layering issues have been found and fixed one at a time, but nobody's swept every modal in the app for the same class of bug — the syllabus modal, both faculty pickers, import, notifications, the account menu, search. Worth specifically reserving a z-index tier for the case of a modal opened from inside another modal, like the faculty picker launched from within the import flow, since that's exactly the kind of moment this bug tends to resurface in.

The whole demo's believability rests on the world being pinned to one fixed moment with no randomness anywhere in the render path — that needs to be checked deliberately, not assumed. Worth testing specifically from a browser in a different timezone than the server, since that's the kind of mismatch that produces a silent hydration difference between what the server rendered and what the browser expects, without ever throwing an obvious error.

For an actual deployment, the role-picker-plus-email flow should collapse into a single BRACU SSO login that already knows who the person is. Worth deciding now how a person who genuinely holds two roles gets handled — a faculty member who also coordinates part-time, or a TA who's technically still a student — because the current model assumes one person maps to exactly one role, and that assumption won't survive contact with a real university.

Nothing in the product today addresses keyboard navigation, screen-reader labeling, or contrast ratios, despite the "registrar-grade" bar the product holds itself to — a university's IT or accessibility office will ask about this before signing anything. Worth specifically checking the Momentum rings and the grade-distribution charts, since both currently communicate meaning through color alone; a colorblind student needs a pattern or a label there, not just a different shade of green or red.

Live class and Record are fully designed on the front end but have no real video service behind them — Agora, LiveKit, or a similar provider needs to be wired in before any real class can run on this. Worth planning the outage case from the start: if the video backend itself goes down mid-class, does the experience degrade gracefully to audio or a promised recorded catch-up, or does the class simply fail with no explanation to the students still sitting in it.

Section: A Real LLM and Retrieval Pipeline
Feedback/Query: Tutor, Copilot, and Analyst are currently scripted rather than genuinely grounded, and connecting a real model with retrieval over actual uploaded course material — plus the usage-cap governance the product already promises — is the core of turning this into a real product rather than a convincing demo. The corner case that will actually surface in a pilot: a course with thin uploaded material will make the Tutor look noticeably worse than a well-resourced one, for reasons that have nothing to do with model quality. Worth setting a minimum-content bar before Tutor is turned on for a given course, so a sparse course doesn't produce embarrassing "not covered" answers on material a student reasonably expects it to know.

Section: BRACU SSO and the Student Information System
Feedback/Query: Real identity and a real roster and grade-posting pipeline are the actual gating item before any pilot can run, well ahead of any UI work. Worth deciding the reconciliation process up front for a SIS record with a name or ID typo, or a late add/drop that hasn't synced yet — a mismatch there breaks both the "find yourself" moment on the front end and the eligibility and certification pipeline underneath it.

For deadlines and live-class alerts, a WhatsApp Business API or a local SMS gateway would reach students far more reliably than an in-app bell ever will, matching how they actually expect to be reminded of things. At more than six thousand students, worth putting the same kind of usage-cap governance around message volume that already exists for AI spend — an unbounded messaging bill is exactly the kind of surprise the product goes out of its way to avoid on the AI side, and it shouldn't reappear here by oversight.

Letting a student push their schedule and deadlines into Google Calendar or Outlook with one click is a small, cheap addition with outsized daily-use value. Worth handling the reschedule case properly — if a class moves rooms or changes teacher mid-term, the synced calendar entry needs to update automatically, or a student ends up trusting a calendar event that's quietly gone stale.

Wiring in a plagiarism-detection tool for assignment submissions is a standard expectation for an academic platform at this point. It needs a clear policy for two specific cases though: group submissions, where one member's overlap shouldn't automatically flag the whole team, and legitimately shared starter code that a teacher hands out — false positives against provided boilerplate would erode trust in the check very quickly.

Shikho already has a K-12 and exam-prep content library and real brand trust across Bangladesh, and it's worth checking whether relevant foundational material can cross into Campus rather than building everything from scratch for BRAC. The thing that would undermine this if done carelessly: BRAC's CSE curriculum has its own sequencing and terminology, so any imported content needs to be mapped precisely to the right course and topic rather than bulk-dropped in — a generic-feeling import would work directly against the "built on your reality" pitch this whole product is making.

There's currently no product analytics in place at all, and without it there will be no way to show BRAC, at renewal time, that anyone actually used what they paid for. Worth designing the event tracking with the same guardrail already applied to Momentum in mind — instrumentation is exactly the kind of infrastructure that could accidentally expose a teacher's private activity data to an aggregate dashboard if it isn't scoped deliberately from the start.

Section: Migrating From What BRACU Uses Today
Feedback/Query: Neither the product nor the underlying document says what happens to whatever system BRACU currently runs on — existing content, rosters, historical grades — and that's usually the first practical question a real buyer asks once a demo has already landed well. Worth deciding specifically whether historical grade records migrate as a read-only archive or as live editable data, since those two paths carry very different integrity and audit requirements, and getting this wrong risks an actual transcript discrepancy for a real student down the line.
